title: Recognize agency beyond completion
summary: Notice your teen's useful choices and adjustments even when the larger task remains unfinished.

details.content: Recognizing only completed work can leave other important acts unnoticed. Naming help-seeking, adaptation, or a deliberate pause gives your teen more ways to experience agency. Care and connection remain available regardless of performance.
Instead of saying, "You still didn't finish," try, "The work is unfinished, and you also asked for clarification before you became overwhelmed." Address what remains needed at a more useful time.

content: Choose one useful process to notice.
Name the specific action your teen took.
Allow completion and process to count together.
Keep recognition when the larger task remains unfinished.
Keep warmth, help, and basic needs independent of performance.

title: Make recognition specific and chosen
summary: Use accurate, proportionate recognition or an agreed reward that your teen actually finds welcome.

details.content: A response becomes reinforcing when it makes a useful action more likely to occur again. What feels rewarding can differ between people and moments, so ask what lands. Ordinary recognition, relief, privacy, or an enjoyable ending may be more welcome than enthusiastic praise.
Instead of saying, "You're finally being responsible," try, "You asked for company before getting stuck; would you prefer that I acknowledge it quietly or leave the moment alone?"

content: Ask what kind of acknowledgment feels welcome.
Describe the action rather than grading identity.
Keep the response close in time to the useful act.
Keep recognition proportionate and avoid comparison.
Honor an agreed reward without adding another demand.

title: Design a winnable MEET encounter
summary: Plan meaning, environment, entry, and terms with your teen before a difficult encounter.

details.content: MEET is the manual's calm-time planning tool for creating a workable encounter. Meaning, environment, entry, and terms help you preserve choice while reducing avoidable friction. A useful challenge requires some effort while leaving adjustment and stopping available.

Instead of announcing, "We'll work until the project is done," try, "Would you like to agree on a first step, the company you want, and where we stop?" Shape the plan together if your teen wants your involvement.

content: Ask permission to plan together.
Find a purpose your teen values or accepts.
Reduce one source of environmental friction.
Define a small, visible entry your teen finds credible.
Agree on support, duration, stopping, and what follows.

title: Keep the agreed ending
summary: Honor the stopping rule and pleasant ending so a small start does not become a moving target.

details.content: A real stopping rule makes the encounter more predictable. Adding more work after an agreed effort can make the next invitation harder to trust. Let the ending happen as agreed, and discuss future work separately.
Instead of saying, "That went well; now do the rest," try, "That's the point we agreed to stop." Let the agreed break happen without a fresh condition.

content: Define enough before the attempt begins.
Honor the stopping point when it arrives.
Let the agreed break or pleasant activity occur.
Avoid increasing the task because one attempt went well.
Discuss further work in a separate, agreed conversation.

title: Adjust without taking over
summary: Use the least support that keeps the encounter workable while preserving your teen's choices.

details.content: Taking over may create immediate movement and make you more likely to take over again. That short-term relief can obscure whether your teen has room to direct the encounter. Notice your urgency and offer one adjustment before adding more control.
Instead of taking the laptop and reorganizing the assignment, try, "Would a smaller step, a quieter space, or stopping for now help?" Accept the choice and reduce your involvement if your teen asks.

content: Notice when your own urgency is increasing.
Ask what kind of involvement your teen wants.
Offer one adjustment at a time.
Use the least support that remains workable.
Stop or change approach when your involvement adds pressure.

title: Build a variety of positive experiences
summary: Create opportunities for agency through interest, contribution, connection, imperfect action, and recovery as well as tasks.

details.content: If every supported experience concerns schoolwork or chores, support may feel like another productivity system. The manual includes joy, contribution, repair, and return as experiences worth protecting. Ask what matters to your teen and make room for different kinds of success.

Instead of making drawing time a reward that must be earned through homework, try, "Would you like some uninterrupted time for the drawing you've been enjoying?" Let the interest matter in its own right.

content: Include an activity chosen for interest or enjoyment.
Offer opportunities for genuine contribution.
Make room for a rough or incomplete first version.
Recognize help-seeking, deliberate pauses, return, and repair.
Protect connection and enjoyment from becoming performance tests.

title: Learn from an unfinished attempt
summary: Acknowledge the remaining task while preserving the useful action and redesigning later.

details.content: An unfinished task can have practical consequences while still containing a useful act of agency. Retroactively erasing that act makes recognition depend on completion again. Later, use the experience to change one condition instead of assigning a character judgment.
Instead of saying, "The whole plan failed because you stopped," try, "The task is unfinished, and you noticed the overload early." Leave the redesign for a calmer time when your teen is willing.

content: Name what remains unfinished without minimizing consequences.
Keep conclusions specific to the situation.
Recognize the useful action that actually occurred.
Wait until the moment is calm enough to redesign.
Change one condition for a later attempt together.

title: Review and fade support collaboratively
summary: Use a light practice cycle to learn what helps and transfer direction as your teen finds it workable.

details.content: A modest cycle gives you time to learn from a few encounters without constantly replacing the system. Review conditions and pressure rather than scoring the person. Fading means transferring useful functions with your teen's involvement, while support can remain available where wanted.
Instead of declaring, "You managed twice, so you're on your own now," try, "Which parts would you like to handle yourself, and what support should stay?" Try one agreed change before reviewing again.

content: Choose one situation and one agency target.
Try a few low-pressure encounters before increasing difficulty.
Record helpful conditions only in a way your teen accepts.
Review what felt useful and what felt like pressure.
Transfer choice and planning gradually while retaining wanted support.
